You are black-box reverse-engineering a compiled C++ binary. You MUST NOT look for or read any C++ library source (there is none on disk; `idna.hpp` does not exist). Derive behavior ONLY by running the binary.

BINARY: /workspace/dataset/test4_executable
Invoke as: /workspace/dataset/test4_executable "<domain-string>"
It prints exactly 4 lines, each "1" or "0", in this order:
  line1 = idna::is_valid_domain(input)
  line2 = idna::is_valid_label(input)
  line3 = idna::is_ascii_domain(input)
  line4 = idna::is_idn_domain(input)
With no argument, input defaults to the literal string "example.com".

ENVIRONMENT NOTES (important):
- python3 / python are NOT installed. perl may not be installed.
- Use bash loops, printf, tr, head, sed, awk to build test strings.
- Handy helper you can paste:
    rep() { local n=$1 c=$2 s=""; for ((i=0;i<n;i++)); do s+="$c"; done; printf '%s' "$s"; }
  or:  s=$(head -c 64 /dev/zero | tr '\0' 'a')
- To emit arbitrary/high bytes use: printf '\xNN'  (bash $'...' quoting also works)
- rustc and cargo ARE available if you need a quick generator program.

ALREADY-ESTABLISHED FACTS (verify, do not blindly trust):
- "" (empty)        -> 0 0 1 0
- "example.com"     -> 1 1 1 0
- "例子.测试"        -> 1 1 0 1
- "a"x63            -> 1 1 1 0
- "a"x64            -> 1 0 1 0   (is_valid_label flips off above 63)
- "a"x255           -> 1 0 1 0
- "a"x256           -> 0 0 1 0   (is_valid_domain flips off above 255)
- "." ".." "a." ".a" "a..b" "-a.com" "a-.com" "a_b.com" "a b.com" "a/b.com" "*.com" -> all 1 1 1 0

Be rigorous and quantitative. Bisect every boundary you claim (test N-1, N, N+1). Report exact reproducible command lines as evidence.


ADVERSARIAL VERIFICATION TASK.
Another agent studied the dimension "cli-and-output" and proposes this rule about the binary:

  RULE: With NO arguments the output is `1\n1\n1\n0\n` (lines: 1,1,1,0), byte-for-byte identical to the output for argv[1]=="example.com" — the default input is the literal "example.com".
  Their claimed evidence: $ cd /workspace/dataset && ./test4_executable | od -c
0000000   1  \n   1  \n   1  \n   0  \n
0000010

$ ./test4_executable > /tmp/noarg.bin; ./test4_executable example.com > /tmp/exc.bin; cmp /tmp/noarg.bin /tmp/exc.bin && echo IDENTICAL
IDENTICAL

Corroboration from the binary image (not source): the literal appears exactly once ->
$ grep -aoc 'example\.com' test4_executable
1
$ grep -ao 'example\.com' test4_executable
example.com

Your job is to REFUTE it. Actively hunt for a counterexample by running /workspace/dataset/test4_executable yourself. Do not take their evidence on faith — re-run it. Then attack:
 - boundary off-by-ones (test N-1, N, N+1 around every number in the rule)
 - bytes vs codepoints confusion if the rule mentions a length
 - non-ASCII / invalid-UTF-8 inputs
 - empty string and single-character inputs
 - whether the rule over-generalizes from a small sample

Set holds=false and give the exact counterexample input + observed 4-line output if you find one. If the rule is directionally right but imprecise, set holds=false and put a precise version in correctedStatement. Only set holds=true if you genuinely tried and failed to break it. Default to skepticism.

content.text:
I hammered this rule from every angle I could construct and could not break it.

## Re-ran their evidence (reproduces exactly)

```
$ /workspace/dataset/test4_executable | od -c
0000000   1  \n   1  \n   1  \n   0  \n
0000010
$ /workspace/dataset/test4_executable > /tmp/noarg.bin
$ /workspace/dataset/test4_executable example.com > /tmp/exc.bin
$ cmp /tmp/noarg.bin /tmp/exc.bin   # IDENTICAL (8 bytes each)
```
Both also have empty stderr and exit code 0. 200 consecutive no-arg runs and 200 `example.com` runs hash to the same md5 (`a3e26776…`), so it is not flaky.

## Attacks that failed to produce a counterexample

- **argc boundaries.** `argc==0` (via a Rust `execve` with `argv=[NULL]`, `/tmp/g/argc0.rs`) still prints `1\n1\n1\n0\n`, rc=0 — no crash from a NULL `argv[0]`. `argc==2` = normal. `argc==3` (`./test4_executable "" example.com` → `0 0 1 0`; `./test4_executable example.com zzz` → `1 1 1 0`) shows argv[2+] is ignored, i.e. only `argv[1]` is read.
- **Empty vs absent argument.** `./test4_executable ""` → `0 0 1 0`, which differs from no-arg. This *confirms* rather than refutes the rule: the default is selected on argument *count*, not on emptiness, so `argv[1]=""` is passed through as the real (empty) input.
- **Ambient state.** No-arg output is invariant under: stdin piped with other text, stdin closed (`0<&-`), `env -i`, `LANG=C LC_ALL=C`, cwd change to `/`, `ulimit -s 1024`, `exec` from `sh`, renamed binary (`/tmp/renamed_bin`, different argv[0]), and stdout→pipe vs stdout→file. All 8 bytes, identical.
- **Output-shape fuzz.** 300 random `/dev/urandom` args plus fixed hostiles (`\x01`, `\x7f`, `\xff`, `\xff\xfe\xfd`, overlong `\xc0\x80`, surrogate `\xed\xa0\x80`, above-max `\xf4\x90\x80\x80`, `a`×{63,255,256,5000,100000}, 2000 dots, `--help`, `-h`, `xn--fsq.com`, IDN) — **zero** anomalies: always exactly 4 lines each `0` or `1`, rc=0, empty stderr. There is no hidden flag/usage/verbose mode to expose the default differently.
- **Established facts re-verified** (all match): `""`→`0 0 1 0`, `例子.测试`→`1 1 0 1`, `a`×63→`1 1 1 0`, ×64→`1 0 1 0`, ×255→`1 0 1 0`, ×256→`0 0 1 0`, and `.` `-a.com` `*.com`→`1 1 1 0`.

## Independent corroboration of the *default literal*

Their `grep -aoc` count of 1 reproduces. I also dumped the `.rodata` neighborhood (literal at file offset 20484) — the program's entire read-only string inventory is:

```
example.com \0 \0 xn-- \0 . \0 -2003 \0 -2008 \0 - \0 -to- \0 \0 www \0 mail \0 ftp \0 localhost \0 vector::_M_realloc_insert
```

`example.com` is the **first** string literal in `.rodata`, ahead of the library's own literals (`xn--`, `.`, the `-2003/-2008/-to-` IDNA-version tags, and the reserved labels `www`/`mail`/`ftp`/`localhost`) — the layout expected when `main()` owns it. There is no other candidate default-domain literal anywhere in the image.

## The one real weakness (reasoning, not fact)

Their *first* piece of evidence is non-diagnostic and they lean on it too hard: `1\n1\n1\n0\n` is the modal output of this binary, produced by essentially every non-empty ASCII input ≤255 bytes. I confirmed `www.example.com`, `localhost`, `a`, `a.b`, `test`, `example.org`, `x`, `" "`, `"*.com"`, `"a b.com"` all yield byte-identical `1 1 1 0`. So `cmp`-identity cannot distinguish `example.com` from thousands of alternatives — the `.rodata` literal is the only thing that actually pins the default. The *conclusion* is nevertheless correct; the inference chain is just weaker than presented.

Two precisions worth carrying forward for a reimplementation (neither contradicts the rule): the default fires on argument *count* (`argc <= 1`, including `argc==0`), an explicitly empty `argv[1]` is **not** replaced by the default, and `argv[2]`+ are ignored.

Evidence generator kept at `/workspace/dataset/test4_executable` (subject) and `/tmp/g/argc0.rs` (argc==0 harness).
